questions.stem: How is sleep linked to mental health?
options: Sleep problems are caused only by mental illness, never the reverse
Poor sleep can worsen mood, and poor mood can disrupt sleep
Sleep affects physical health only and has no link with mood
Mental health problems always improve when people sleep less
questions.explanation: The relationship runs both ways: sleep loss increases irritability, anxiety and low mood, while conditions such as depression and anxiety often disturb sleep.

questions.stem: According to the repair and restoration theory, we sleep in order to:
options: conserve energy at times when food is hard to find
allow the body and brain to recover and repair after the day
stay safe from predators at times when activity is dangerous
process and strengthen memories formed during the day
questions.explanation: The repair and restoration theory proposes that sleep lets the body replenish energy and repair tissue, and the brain recover. Staying safe and saving energy are evolutionary explanations; memory processing is the consolidation theory.

questions.stem: Which observation supports the repair and restoration theory?
options: Animals sleep more when food is scarce
Growth hormone release rises in deep sleep
Prey animals tend to sleep less than predators
People remember word lists better after sleeping
questions.explanation: Release of growth hormone, which supports tissue growth and repair, peaks in deep sleep, consistent with a restorative function. The other findings relate to evolutionary and consolidation explanations.

questions.stem: The evolutionary theory of sleep proposes that:
options: sleep evolved mainly to clear waste products that build up in the brain
sleep evolved so that memories could be moved from short-term to long-term storage
sleep evolved only in humans as a result of complex brain development
sleep evolved to keep animals safe and conserve energy when activity is risky
questions.explanation: The evolutionary theory sees sleep as adaptive: inactivity at times when an animal cannot find food efficiently or is vulnerable to predators improves survival.

questions.stem: Large grazing animals such as horses sleep only a few hours a day, while predators such as lions sleep much longer. Which theory explains this best?
options: the information consolidation theory, because grazers form fewer memories each day
the clean-up theory, because grazers produce much less waste in the brain
the evolutionary theory, because prey must stay alert and feed for long periods
the repair and restoration theory, because grazing animals need less tissue repair
questions.explanation: Prey animals are vulnerable while asleep and need many hours to eat low-energy food, so short sleep is adaptive. Predators are safer and can meet their needs quickly, so they can afford to sleep longer.

questions.stem: Students who learn a list of words and then sleep recall more of them than students who stay awake for the same time. Which theory does this support?
options: repair and restoration theory
evolutionary theory
clean-up theory
information consolidation theory
questions.explanation: The information consolidation theory proposes that sleep helps process and strengthen memories formed while awake. Better recall after sleep is consistent with this.

questions.stem: The clean-up theory of sleep proposes that:
options: sleep allows the body to rebuild muscle tissue that was damaged during the day
sleep allows the animal to avoid predators during the most dangerous hours
sleep allows the brain to transfer memories into long-term storage
sleep allows waste that builds up in the brain while awake to be cleared
questions.explanation: Research in mice found that waste clearance from the brain increases during sleep, through a fluid-based system sometimes called the glymphatic system. This suggests sleep helps remove potentially harmful substances such as beta-amyloid.

questions.stem: Why do many psychologists argue that no single theory fully explains the need for sleep?
options: Sleep has been shown to have no function in human beings
Each has some evidence, and sleep may serve several functions
None of the theories has any evidence supporting it at all
All the theories make exactly the same predictions about sleep
questions.explanation: There is evidence for restoration, survival, memory consolidation and waste clearance. These explanations are not mutually exclusive, so sleep probably serves several purposes.

questions.stem: Which is a personal factor that can contribute to sleep deprivation?
options: using a phone in bed late at night
a society where shops open 24 hours
an early school start time
an employer's roster of night shifts
questions.explanation: Personal factors are within the individual's control or circumstances, such as screen use, caffeine, stress or study habits. Opening hours, school start times and rosters are societal or organisational factors.

questions.stem: Which is a societal factor that contributes to sleep deprivation?
options: shift work and a 24-hour economy
drinking coffee in the late afternoon
worrying about a test the next day
keeping a television in the bedroom
questions.explanation: Societal factors come from how society and work are organised, such as shift work, long working hours and services available around the clock. The other options are personal factors.

questions.stem: Shift workers often report poorer sleep and more health problems. Which explanation is most likely?
options: Night work conflicts with the body's natural timing of sleep
Shift workers need far less sleep than people who work during the day
Daytime sleep is always longer and deeper than night-time sleep
Shift work affects only physical health and never mental health
questions.explanation: Night shifts require people to be awake when the body is primed to sleep and to sleep in daylight and noise. This shortens and disrupts sleep, which is linked to fatigue, accidents and poorer mental health.

questions.stem: Adolescents are often sleep deprived on school nights. Which combination of factors best explains this?
options: a reduced effect of evening light and screens on their alertness
a natural shift to later sleep times plus early school starts
a natural need for much less sleep than children or adults
an inability to fall asleep at any time before midnight
questions.explanation: During adolescence the body's sleep timing shifts later, so teenagers feel sleepy later at night, but school and other commitments still require early waking. Screens, homework and social activities add to the loss.

questions.stem: A study finds that drivers who have slept less than five hours are more likely to have crashes. Which conclusion is most justified?
options: Drivers who sleep more than five hours never have any crashes
Crash risk is unrelated to how alert a driver is
Sleep loss is linked with crash risk, supporting adequate sleep
Sleep loss is the only cause of car crashes in the population studied
questions.explanation: The study shows an association, consistent with sleep loss impairing attention and reaction time. It does not show sleep loss is the only cause, and other drivers still have crashes.

questions.stem: Which is a personal strategy to improve sleep quality?
options: using a laptop in bed to relax before sleeping
sleeping in for several hours on weekends
keeping a regular sleep and wake time every day
drinking an energy drink to stay alert in the evening
questions.explanation: A consistent schedule helps keep the body's sleep timing stable. Caffeine, screens in bed and large weekend sleep-ins tend to disrupt sleep.

questions.stem: Which is an organisational strategy to increase employees' sleep duration?
options: requiring staff to answer emails late into the night
scheduling meetings early after night shifts end
rosters that limit consecutive night shifts
asking employees to drink more coffee during shifts
questions.explanation: Organisations can help by limiting long or consecutive night shifts, allowing recovery time and setting reasonable hours. Expecting late-night availability reduces sleep.

questions.stem: Some schools have moved to later start times. What is the main reason, based on sleep research?
options: It gives teachers more time to mark work before classes begin
It reduces the total number of hours students spend at school
It ensures students go to bed earlier on school nights
It fits teenagers' later sleep timing, so they sleep longer
questions.explanation: Because adolescents' sleep timing shifts later, a later start allows more sleep before school. Studies have linked later starts with longer sleep and better alertness.

questions.stem: A student has trouble falling asleep. Which advice is most consistent with good sleep hygiene?
options: exercise vigorously just before getting into bed each night
stay in bed awake for as long as it takes to fall asleep
avoid screens and caffeine before bed; keep the room dark
nap for two hours after school to make up for lost sleep
questions.explanation: Sleep hygiene includes limiting caffeine and screens in the evening, keeping the bedroom dark, quiet and cool, and having a wind-down routine. Long naps and intense exercise close to bedtime can make falling asleep harder.

questions.stem: A person working night shifts sleeps during the day but keeps waking because of traffic noise and daylight. Which personal strategy is most likely to help?
options: sleeping in short naps scattered through the whole day
blackout curtains and earplugs to make the room dark and quiet
a large meal and strong coffee just before going to bed
keeping a bright light on so the body adjusts to sleeping in light
questions.explanation: A dark, quiet environment supports sleep at any time of day. Caffeine before bed and bright light promote wakefulness, and scattered naps give fragmented, poorer-quality sleep.

questions.stem: In psychology, stress is best described as:
options: a disorder that requires medication to be treated successfully
the feeling of calm that follows the removal of a threat
arousal when demands are seen as exceeding one's resources
any event that occurs in a person's life, whether good or bad
questions.explanation: Stress is a physiological and psychological response that occurs when a person perceives that demands are greater than their ability to cope. A stressor is the event that triggers it.

questions.stem: Which is a stressor rather than a stress response?
options: difficulty concentrating
feeling irritable and tense
a looming assignment deadline
a racing, pounding heart
questions.explanation: A stressor is the source of stress, such as a deadline. A racing heart, poor concentration and irritability are physiological, cognitive and emotional responses to it.

questions.stem: The fight-or-flight response is activated by which division of the nervous system?
options: the somatic nervous system
the central nervous system only
the sympathetic nervous system
the parasympathetic nervous system
questions.explanation: The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for action, with increased heart rate, breathing and release of adrenaline. The parasympathetic system calms the body afterwards.

questions.stem: In which situation is the fight-or-flight response most likely to have a positive effect on health and safety?
options: lying awake for weeks worrying about money
feeling tense every day in a job with constant conflict
sitting in heavy traffic every morning for months
jumping out of the way of a car that suddenly swerves
questions.explanation: Fight-or-flight is adaptive for brief, immediate physical threats, giving energy and speed. When it is triggered repeatedly by ongoing psychological stressors, it can harm health.

questions.stem: Why might the fight-or-flight response be harmful when it is triggered by modern stressors such as exams or workplace conflict?
options: The body readies for action that never comes, and repeated activation strains it
The response cannot be triggered by psychological stressors, so it has no effect on the body
The response permanently switches off the parasympathetic nervous system
The response lowers heart rate and blood pressure, which leads to fatigue
questions.explanation: Psychological stressors rarely require running or fighting, so the energy and arousal are not used. Repeated activation over time is linked to raised blood pressure, weakened immunity and other health problems.

questions.stem: What are the three stages of Selye's general adaptation syndrome, in order?
options: resistance, alarm reaction, exhaustion
alarm reaction, exhaustion, resistance
shock, countershock, recovery
alarm reaction, resistance, exhaustion
questions.explanation: Selye described an alarm reaction, then resistance as the body tries to cope, then exhaustion if the stressor continues. Shock and countershock are two phases within the alarm reaction.

questions.stem: In the shock phase of the alarm reaction, the body's resistance to stress:
options: falls to zero and the person collapses
drops below its normal level
rises well above its normal level
stays at its normal level
questions.explanation: In shock, the body briefly responds as if injured, and resistance falls below normal. In countershock, the sympathetic nervous system activates and resistance rises above normal.

questions.stem: During the resistance stage of the general adaptation syndrome:
options: resistance stays above normal as cortisol helps the body cope
resistance falls below normal and illness becomes very likely
the body returns to its normal state and the stressor disappears
the body responds as if injured and blood pressure drops
questions.explanation: In resistance, stress hormones such as cortisol keep the body coping with the stressor, so resistance is above normal. Resources are being used up, which can leave the person more vulnerable to other stressors.

questions.stem: A nurse has worked long shifts in a chronically understaffed ward for many months. She now gets sick often and feels drained. Using Selye's model, which stage is she most likely in, and why?
options: countershock, because her resistance has risen above normal
exhaustion, because prolonged stress has depleted her resources
resistance, because her body is coping well with the stressor
alarm reaction, because the stressor has only just begun
questions.explanation: After prolonged resistance, the body's resources are depleted and resistance falls below normal, leading to fatigue and stress-related illness. Frequent illness after months of stress fits exhaustion.

questions.stem: Which is a long-term effect of stress that Selye's model helps explain?
options: increased vulnerability to illness as the immune system is weakened
permanent improvement in the body's ability to resist infection
complete protection from future stressors after one stressful event
a reduction in stress hormones during prolonged stress
questions.explanation: Prolonged stress keeps stress hormones elevated, which over time suppresses immune functioning and strains the body. This explains why chronic stress is linked to illness.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of Selye's general adaptation syndrome?
options: It proposes that each type of stressor produces a completely different response
It ignores how a person's appraisal of a stressor shapes the response
It explains only psychological responses and ignores the body's physiology
It was based mainly on studies of large groups of human volunteers
questions.explanation: Selye's model describes a general physiological response and largely ignores psychological factors, such as how people interpret a stressor. Much of his research was with rats, and he proposed the same response regardless of stressor.

questions.stem: Problem-focused coping involves:
options: taking steps to change the source of stress
managing the emotions produced by a stressor
avoiding thinking about the stressor at all
using alcohol to forget about the stressor
questions.explanation: Problem-focused coping targets the stressor itself, through actions such as planning, time management and seeking information. Managing emotions is emotion-focused coping.

questions.stem: Which is an example of emotion-focused coping?
options: going for a run to ease tension after a fight
making a study timetable for an upcoming exam
asking a teacher to explain a difficult concept
negotiating a later deadline with a manager
questions.explanation: Emotion-focused coping reduces the emotional distress caused by a stressor without changing the stressor itself. The other options all tackle the problem directly.

questions.stem: When is emotion-focused coping likely to be more useful than problem-focused coping?
options: when the stressor can be solved by planning, such as an exam
when the person has plenty of time and resources to fix the problem
when the stressor is a simple task that needs to be organised
when the stressor cannot be changed, such as the death of a relative
questions.explanation: Problem-focused coping works best when something can be done about the stressor. When it is uncontrollable, managing the emotional response helps more.

questions.stem: A student overwhelmed by assignments makes a schedule and also uses relaxation breathing when she feels panicky. Which statement best describes her approach?
options: She combines problem-focused and emotion-focused coping
She relies only on emotion-focused coping
She relies only on problem-focused coping
She uses avoidance rather than any coping
questions.explanation: Making a schedule addresses the stressor, which is problem-focused, while relaxation breathing manages her distress, which is emotion-focused. Using both is often the most effective approach.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of relying only on emotion-focused strategies such as avoidance or distraction?
options: They always increase physiological arousal straight away
They require the person to change their job or school
The source of stress remains and may get worse over time
They are never helpful in any stressful situation at all
questions.explanation: Emotion-focused strategies can give relief, but if the stressor can be changed, avoiding it may allow it to grow. Some emotion-focused strategies, such as exercise or meditation, are healthy.

questions.stem: Burnout refers to:
options: a brief surge of energy that occurs during the alarm reaction
a sleep disorder in which a person cannot fall asleep at night
the immediate fear response to a sudden, life-threatening event
emotional depletion and loss of motivation from chronic stressors
questions.explanation: Burnout is the exhaustion, cynicism and reduced motivation that develop when people face prolonged stress, often at work. It is commonly reported in demanding caring roles such as nursing and teaching.

questions.stem: Which stress-management strategy is problem-focused?
options: meditation to feel much calmer
exercise to release tension
talking to a friend to vent
time management to plan tasks
questions.explanation: Time management changes how the person deals with the demands themselves, so it is problem-focused. Meditation, exercise and venting reduce the emotional effects of stress.
